To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Hypertension is the most common cardiovascular abnormality in aircrew; 2) Hypertension in aircrew is more common in the older population and in females; 3) Hypertension may cause cardiovascular and cerebrovascular complications; 4) Hypertensive aircrew are at risk for orthostatic hypovolaemia and hypotension; and, 5) Hypertensive and hypotensive aircrew should be carefully monitored for cardiovascular complications.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a comprehensive and integrated approach to the problem of hypertension and orthostatic intolerance in aircrew.
the development of a system for the detection and treatment of hypertension in flight personnel and the development of a method for the long-term monitoring of the blood pressure of aircrew members.

the evaluation of blood pressure in aircrew members, with the diagnosis of labile hypertension and orthostatic intolerance in aircrew, and with the development of a new method of non-invasive measurement of blood pressure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the current blood pressure standards for flying personnel are not based on sound scientific data.
the current air force standards for hypertension are too conservative and that they should be liberalized. This is particularly important for older aircrew members.
hypertension in itself does not preclude flying, but that it should be considered in the context of the individual and his or her medical history.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk of hypertension in aircrew is low and that hypertension in itself is not a contraindication for aircrew.

the diagnosis of hypertension is not the only criterion for exclusion from flying status but that the presence or absence of target organ damage, the type and severity of the hypertension as well as the presence of other diseases are important factors to be considered in the decision to exclude an individual from flying.
the diagnosis of hypertension in the context of aviation medicine is not as easy as it may appear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypertension is not a bar for flying and can be controlled by pharmacological means without affecting flight safety.

orthostatic hypopension should be considered as a risk factor for the development of hypertension and that the presence of hypertension and orthostatic intolerance should not be used to exclude an aircrew applicant.

the prevalence of hypertension is high in aircrew, and that there is an urgent need for a more liberal attitude towards the acceptance of applicants for flying training with labile hypertension and of aircrew with hypertension controlled by anti-hypertension drugs.
